coverage.title: Mexico aviation authority faces FAA safety evaluation
coverage.summary: The Mexican civil aviation authority will undergo US FAA assessment this week on safety standards compliance, with potential consequences for Mexico's aviation category ranking.

events.background: The FAA's IASA program checks whether a country's aviation regulator has the staff, rules and oversight capacity required by the International Civil Aviation Organization. Mexico lost its Category 1 rating in 2021 and has been working since 2023 to regain it.
events.view: A one-week visit will not settle the rating either way, since the specialist quoted expects any conclusion to take at least six months. The relevant comparison is Mexico's three-year record since losing Category 1 in 2023, not this week's visit, so the practical test is whether AFAC can show new inspection staffing and updated regulation rather than a single inspection outcome.
events.prediction: AFAC most likely receives a preliminary readout with a formal decision deferred for months, not an immediate category change. That view fails if the FAA issues any determination, positive or negative, within the six-month window the specialist named.

The group calculates that exempting Mexican extrusions wou

coverage.title: US aluminum industry opposes tariff exemptions for Mexico and Canada in USMCA renegotiation
coverage.summary: The Coalition for a Prosperous America has urged US Treasury and US trade office to reject downstream aluminum exemptions for Mexico and Canada in the USMCA review and raise tariffs on fabricated products.

events.background: Section 232 tariffs on metals sit outside USMCA and can theoretically be applied regardless of the trade pact's origin rules, which is why the aluminum lobby wants the two kept separate rather than allowing USMCA-qualified Mexican extrusions to bypass the 50% metals duty.
events.view: The Coalition's own numbers show why this fight matters to producers: a landed cost gap of US$2.39 versus US$3.88 per pound, about 38%, would price US extrusion makers out of contracts if Mexico wins an exemption. Mexico's ask is not free, either, since exporters have already paid close to US$23 billion in tariffs in the year through April 2026, so an exemption would reverse a cost that has been real and recent, not hypothetical.
events.prediction: The more likely outcome is a narrower compromise, such as quotas or partial relief tied to origin verification, rather than a full exemption or a full rejection. That expectation would be wrong if USTR or Treasury issues a blanket ruling either exempting Mexican and Canadian aluminum entirely or explicitly rejecting any relief.

coverage.title: US money-transfer rule near Mexico border damages small businesses
coverage.summary: The Trump administration's April rule targeting cartel money-laundering has caused unintended economic harm to legitimate small companies along the US-Mexico border, affecting business operations and cash flows.

events.background: The rule cut the cash-transaction reporting threshold for financial-services businesses near the border from $10,000 to $200, sweeping in ordinary grocery-store transfer counters used by immigrant families to pay bills and send money home.
events.view: The mechanism is a data-collection net built for cartel laundering that instead catches small legal businesses lacking compliance staff to handle reporting at that volume. Remittances brought Mexico about $62.47bn in 2025, more than foreign direct investment, and that flow depends on cheap, accessible transfer points like Nachita's staying open. A rule that raises the cost of running those counters shrinks the informal channels households use to move money, without a public estimate of how much cartel activity it actually stops.
events.prediction: Small transfer businesses near the border likely keep absorbing compliance costs or shut down transfer services rather than fight the rule, since litigation is slow and Congress has not acted. That would be wrong if the Treasury narrows the threshold back up or exempts small retailers, which has not been reported.

coverage.title: China imposes preliminary 51.6 percent tariff on Mexican pecan exports
coverage.summary: China's Ministry of Commerce imposed the tariff on Mexican pecan exports citing dumping. Mexico is working to block the measure, which threatens a key agricultural export.

events.background: Mexico exported about $9.1bn total to China in 2024 against $129.5bn in imports, so pecans are a rare Mexican export line into a market where Mexico normally buys, not sells.
events.view: The tariff matters less for Mexico's overall trade, since direct pecan exports to China were $21.9m in 2024, a rounding error next to the roughly $665bn in total Mexican goods exports in 2025 and dwarfed by the $872bn in US-Mexico goods trade. The real exposure is reexports through the United States, which the preliminary ruling explicitly targets by hitting US exporters with a higher 54.3% rate, suggesting China is trying to close a triangulation route rather than punish Mexican producers directly.
events.prediction: Mexico's economy ministry likely negotiates a reduced final rate before the investigation closes, since it has ten days to respond and is already coordinating with the Chinese embassy. That expectation fails if Beijing finalizes rates at or above the 51.6% preliminary level despite the talks.

coverage.title: Mexico appoints financier Roberto Lazzeri as ambassador to United States
coverage.summary: Lazzeri, sent to lead Mexico's most difficult diplomatic front, discusses the future of the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement and regional integration.

events.background: Mexico's president can appoint ambassadors without requiring political or diplomatic background, and Lazzeri's prior finance-ministry and development-bank roles put him in contact with the US Treasury and FinCEN during a 2025 money-laundering dispute involving three Mexican financial institutions.
events.view: Sheinbaum picking a financial technician over a career diplomat signals that the bilateral relationship's hardest problems now run through banking and compliance channels, not conventional diplomacy. That fits a moment when the USMCA review process moves to annual cycles after the US declined a 16-year extension in July 2026, and when disputes over money flows, like the border cash-transfer rule, are already straining the relationship outside trade policy.
events.prediction: Lazzeri's early tenure likely focuses on Treasury and FinCEN relationships rather than broad political outreach, given Sheinbaum's request that he engage the private and financial sectors. That would be wrong if he instead prioritizes congressional or USMCA negotiating rounds over financial-sector diplomacy in his first 100 days.

coverage.title: Mexico's Treasury announces new anti-money-laundering rules effective November 2026
coverage.summary: Mexico's Secretaría de Hacienda has issued modified rules on anti-money-laundering requirements with phased implementation beginning in November 2026.

events.background: The reform amends Mexico's anti-money-laundering law (LFPIORPI), which governs the roughly 120,000 registered individuals and businesses in "vulnerable activities" such as real estate, jewelry and financial services that must report suspicious transactions.
events.view: The shift from a uniform compliance model to a risk-based one lands with a long runway: rules take effect November 30, 2026, main requirements start in 2027, and audits begin only in 2028. That gap matters because Mexico's commercial-bank credit to the private sector is just 35.5% of GDP, so tighter money-laundering oversight targets the formal financial system while informal channels, where 55.2% of workers already operate, remain largely untouched.
events.prediction: Most likely outcome: large firms and financial institutions begin building risk-classification systems well before the 2027 deadline, while smaller registered businesses delay compliance until closer to the 2028 audit start. This would be wrong if Hacienda enforces the November 2026 date more strictly than stated or moves audits earlier.

coverage.title: US ambassador says security agreements will resume avocado operations in Michoacán
coverage.summary: Ronald Johnson said the commitments would strengthen security and allow US government activities to resume immediately in phases.

events.background: Michoacán is Mexico's main avocado export state, and US Department of Agriculture inspectors normally certify orchards there before fruit can cross the border, which is why a security-related suspension halts the trade until Washington judges it safe to send staff back. Avocados sit within the broader US-Mexico goods relationship where about 80% of Mexico's exports go to the United States.
events.view: This is a security concession, not a trade agreement, and it addresses federal-state coordination rather than the extortion and cargo theft that INEGI data shows go unreported 93.2% of the time and fall hardest on small producers who cannot pay for protection. The government's claim of a 46% drop in daily homicides since September 2024 is still preliminary prosecutor data, so a security commitment announced this week rests on figures that could be revised once final death certificates arrive.
events.prediction: US personnel most likely resume avocado-related activity in Michoacán in stages over the coming weeks, with no fixed date given. That would be disproven if Washington re-suspends operations following a new violence alert, which is the same trigger that halted the activity this time.

coverage.title: Mexico wins USMCA arbitration against US investment funds over TV Azteca debt
coverage.summary: A USMCA tribunal rejected a 219 million dollar claim by Cyrus and Contrarian funds against Mexico, ruling the investors were not protected by the trade agreement. The decision spares Mexico from paying disputed bondholder claims.

events.background: USMCA contains an investor-state dispute mechanism that lets foreign investors sue a member government before an independent tribunal if they believe treaty protections were violated, separate from Mexico's domestic courts.
events.view: The ruling closes one specific claim rather than settling how USMCA investor protections apply to sovereign debt disputes generally, since it turned on whether these particular bondholders qualified for protection at all. It also matters for public finances: Mexico is already on the last investment-grade rung at Moody's partly because of Pemex support costs, so avoiding a $219 million payout keeps one more claim off a debt load that rose to 53.2% of GDP in 2025.
events.prediction: The funds are likely to explore appeal routes or alternative legal claims rather than drop the matter, since $219 million is a large sum to abandon after losing on jurisdiction rather than merits. That view would be wrong if Cyrus and Contrarian publicly confirm they are not pursuing further action.

events.background: Under Article 34.7 of the USMCA, the first joint review took place on 1 July 2026 and the US Trade Representative can extend that review process rather than accept the treaty's default 16-year renewal, keeping the pact's future rules unsettled year to year.
events.view: This letter is a signal, not a policy change: 167 House Republicans are backing an extended review, but the review already reverted to annual cycles after the US declined the 16-year extension on 1 July, so the practical trading rules for existing Mexican factories do not shift yet. The people affected are exporters weighing new, long-payback plants, since about 80% of Mexico's exports already depend on the US market and any delay just prolongs the uncertainty they face on future rules of origin.
events.prediction: The joint review process likely continues on its annual track without a firm renewal date, since Congress has no binding vote here, only influence over the Trade Representative's negotiating posture. That would be wrong if Greer's office sets a concrete new review deadline or Mexico and Canada agree to specific concessions this year.

coverage.title: Banxico holds its policy rate at 6.50 percent
coverage.summary: The board left the rate unchanged and said it expects inflation to reach its target in the fourth quarter of 2027.

events.background: Banxico uses the overnight policy rate to influence borrowing and spending. A rate above inflation can slow prices, but it also makes credit more expensive.
events.view: July's inflation report explains the wait. Headline inflation is close to target, but underlying inflation is falling more slowly. Banxico is waiting for that underlying measure to improve before making credit cheaper again.
events.prediction: The next tests will be the September 9 inflation release and the September 24 rate decision. If underlying inflation falls again, a cut becomes more likely. If it reverses, another hold becomes more likely.

coverage.title: Mexico's power system may not meet demand from new factories and data centers
coverage.summary: The report says limited power supply is a bottleneck for new factories, data centers and artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

events.background: A new project needs more than generation. It also needs transmission capacity, a grid connection and reliable power at its site.
events.view: For investors, the immediate risk is whether power will be available at the chosen location and on the investment schedule. Data centers alone could need about 1.5 gigawatts by 2030, while permits and grid connections already slow new supply.
events.prediction: The bottleneck is likely to persist until transmission projects and grid connections move from plans into construction. More completed connection studies and new capacity entering service would weaken that view.

events.title: AI governance challenge emerges as key issue in US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement review
events.why: As the three countries prepare for the trade agreement's review, artificial intelligence regulation and cross-border data governance are emerging as central negotiating topics. Harmonizing AI rules could affect everything from nearshoring investments to data residency requirements.

coverage.title: AI governance challenge emerges as key issue in US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement review
coverage.summary: As the three countries prepare for the trade agreement's review, artificial intelligence regulation and cross-border data governance are emerging as central negotiating topics. Harmonizing AI rules could affect everything from nearshoring investments to data residency requirements.

events.background: Mexico's Senate AI commission is pushing for a dedicated AI chapter as part of the same annual USMCA review process triggered after the US declined the 16-year extension in July 2026, at a time when the US favors light-touch AI rules, Canada is still building its own framework, and Mexico has not settled on a regulatory path.
events.view: A binding AI chapter is unlikely to emerge from this review round, because Mexico still lacks its own AI law to negotiate from and the three countries start from incompatible regulatory philosophies. The proposal matters mainly as a marker for future rounds, since any data-residency or AI rule eventually adopted would affect how foreign-owned factories store and move production data across the border, a live nearshoring concern given how thin new (as opposed to reinvested) foreign investment has been.
events.prediction: Mexico most likely keeps studying AI governance options without a formal chapter appearing in the 2026 review text. That would be wrong if negotiators announce specific AI provisions or a data-governance annex as part of this year's review outcome.

events.why: Oil exports crashed in the first half of 2026, with the most-sold Maya crude down 30.5 percent and Zapoteco recording zero shipments. Pemex's export collapse signals a structural production crisis and reduces a critical source of federal revenue.

coverage.title: Pemex crude oil exports plummet 28 percent, lowest in 36 years
coverage.summary: Oil exports crashed in the first half of 2026, with the most-sold Maya crude down 30.5 percent and Zapoteco recording zero shipments. Pemex's export collapse signals a structural production crisis and reduces a critical source of federal revenue.

events.background: Pemex is not financially separate from the federal government, and its persistent shortfall against Sheinbaum's 1.8 million barrel a day production target is one of the reasons Moody's holds Mexico on the last investment grade rung, citing the cost of propping up the state oil company.
events.view: The export collapse matters less as an oil story than as a fiscal one. Falling exports mean less dollar revenue for a company the state already subsidizes, and every peso spent covering that gap competes with the electricity, water and security spending that new factories need, since broad public debt is already climbing toward near 54.7% of GDP in 2026.
events.prediction: The likely path is more federal support or refinancing for Pemex to offset the lost export revenue, not a near-term production turnaround. That would be wrong if Pemex output moves toward the 1.8 million barrel a day target or exports rebound without additional state backing.
